Satyakam Phukan Guwahati, Assam January, 2006 PROLOGUE The hill tract lying between Bangladesh plains to the south and the Assam plains to the north forms the so called Garo, Khasi and the Jaintia hills, going fom west to east. This range of mountain becomes continous in the east with the Karbi Anglong and North Cachar hills of Assam which itself is connected to the Naga hills in the east. The Garo, Khasi and the Jaintia hills comprises the Indian state having a

Sanskritised name of Meghalaya meaning the abode of the clouds, much alike the Himalayas the home of ice or snow. The Khasi people ie. the Khasi proper and Jaintia and others inhabit the Khasi and Jaintia hills. There are few scattered communities of Khasis in the Karbi Anglong and North Cachar hills districts, Cachar district of Assam and also in Bangladesh. The Khasi country has three parts, the northern Bhoi region with extensive flat lands and valleys, having a gradual sloping towards the north. The central region is called the Ri-Lum. It has a higher elevation and is in the shape of an irregular plateau. The Shillong peak (6449 feet) is the highest point here. It also includes the central plateau of the Jaintia hills with small ranges of hills with wide and beautiful valleys within them. The southern War region is somewhat irregularly composed, having steep slopes, deep gorges, with a sudden descent down to the southern plains. The upper segment of the land presents a temperate climate but the border areas to the north and south have a warmer climate, corresponding to that of the adjacent plainsland. Cherrapunji or Sohra in the Khasi tongue is a rainy spot competitively exchanging place with a neighbouring village of Mawsynram for the title of the 'wettest place on earth’. Khasi is a general term for the various tribes and subtribes of the 1

ekejeqsdeayy jo deur qoyaHS © ae ete Wess ie Asad yTONVd Khasi and Jaintia hills. The Khynriams or Nonglums are the Khasi proper. They inhabit the middle range of hills and are composed of the Khynriam proper and their allied subtribes in the central plateau. The Pnar or Jaintia or Synteng occupy the central plateau of the Jaintia hills. The War sub-tribe live on the south. They include the Shella people and other allied groups, the Amwi people with their allied War-Synteng of the Southern Jaintia hills. The Bhois, both Khasi and Pnar dwell on the northern part of the Khasi and Jaintia hills. Lyngngams comprises a Garo admixed Khasi group dwelling on the westernmost and northwest edge of the Khasi hills. Several minor non-Khasi groups of people are interspersed in between. Majority of the Khasi people are fair and medium complexioned with an Austro-Mongoloid physiognomy and with very common sprinklings of Negroid and Caucasoid features. Khasi proper of the uplands are mostly brown or fair complexion, the Pnars and Bhois are however a bit darker and the Lyngngams a bit more. The overall appearence bear similarities with the Burmese (Myanmarese), Cambodian (Kampuchean), Malay and Palaung-Wa group of people of south-east Asia. However slanting eyes with prominent epicanthic folds and high check bones are less common and less pronounced in the Khasi's physical features, unlike the Mongoloids.

The Khasis practice a system of matriliny. The inheritance of the clanshood coming down the mother's side. This is a peculiarity which is not common with others. Most tribes and communities in the India's north-east are patrilineal. Those few among others to follow the system of matrilineage probably did so after coming in contact with the Khasis like the Hill Lalung or Hill Tiwa tribe of Assam and Meghalaya and the Garos of Meghalaya. The Khasis were in the habit of raising monoliths as commemorative or religious structures. These can be seen strewn all over the Khasi country in the form of menhirs, dolmens and other megaliths. The Konyak Naga tribe also used to indulge in 3 similar activities of erecting monoliths. A linguistic connection was noted by some scholars between the Khasi and Konyak languages and also with the Wanchoo (Vanchoo) tribe of Arunachal Pradesh state of India. The Khasi language alongwith it's various local variations is classed as an Austric language of the Mon-Khmer/Mon-Annam group. The Mon or Tailang are one of the earliest inhabitants of Burma (Myanmar) and represent an Austro-Asiatic segment of people admixed with early Telegu or Telinga immigrants from India. Khmer is another name for the Cambodians or Kampucheans. Annamese are the Vietnamese proper. They also show similarities with the Malay language and a similarity is highly probable with the Malagasy people of the Madagascar island, off the coast of Africa in the Indian occean.

Several linguistic and nomeclatural similarities have been noted between many Mon-Khmer speaking tribes of south-east Asia and the Khasis. Tribe names like Stieng and Bahner are congnate with the names Synteng and Pnar. Name of the tribe Wa is similar to the name War. The Wa tribe represents a comparatively primitive people inhabiting a widely scattered area in upper Burma (Myanmar), the Yunnan province of China and Thailand. They are divided into Lawa or "tame Wa", who are mostly Buddhist, adopting Shan (Tai) or Chinese customs and Kawa or the "Wild Wa" who are animist and were politically autonomous until quite recently. A vivid account of the "Wild Wa" of the recent times can be obtained from the book "The Land of Jade" by a Swedish writer Mr. Bertil Lintner. The book was written on a journey through Assam, Nagaland and across the border through Burma (Myanmar) into Thailand. The linguistic similarities are extensive, a few samples are given herewith. The Khasi language also have words dissimilar with the Austric languages and with striking similarity with languages placed far away in Asia, Europe and Africa, which seems more than mere co- incidence. The origin of the word "Khasi" as applicable to the Khasis is also something of a mystery. graush CHANNEL Sketch map of British Isles Scott, Scotland, Kelts David Scott was perhaps one of the first European to have visited the interiors of the Khasi hills. It was he who first initiated negotiations with a powerful Khasi chieftain, the Syiem of Nongkhlaw U Tirot Singh. The purpose was the construction of a north-south spanning road through the Khasi hills. The Assam plains and the eastern Bengal were by this time already within the confines of the British Raj. He travelled up the numerous footpaths known to Khasis as lynti-khasi to attend a conclave of Khasi chiefs. at Nongkhlaw. Employing porters to carry him, he spent three nights on the way to reach Nongkhlaw on the 3rd of November 1826, covering a distance of 60 miles. He was popular with the hillsfolk and has to his credit the introduction of potato, pears, cabbage and beet cultivation in the hills. Mother of U Tirot Singh Ka Ksan Syiem was particularly fond of this foreigner. She saved him during the sudden revolt of the Khasis, by warning him at the dead of a night. At the age of 45 years, Scott ended his life in his beloved Khasi hills at Cherrapunji in August 1831. His grave can be seen even today. Shillong in the central plateau land was made the military headquarters of the British in 1866 and in 1874 it was made the capital of the province of Assam. After the division of the Assam state and the creation of Meghalaya, Shillong has been the capital of

Meghalaya. Enthralled by its natural beauty, Khasi hills in general and Shillong in particular was called by the Britishers "The Scotland of the East". Scotland is the northernmost of the four countries (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) that comprise the United Kingdom. It is a hilly land with a cool climate and has several offshore islands within its boundaries. Divided into four regions Highlands, Lowlands, Southern Uplands and Islands, Scotland 14 makes up roughly one-third of the island of Great Britain. Scotland is the English name, the French, Italian and the Spanish have different terminology for the words Scotland and scotch : Scotland Scotch French Ecosse [ay-KUHSS] ecossais [ay-KUH-SEH] Italian Scozea [SKOH-ts_ yah] scozzese [Skoht-TSEH-seh] Spanish Escocia [ehss-KOH-S_ yah] escosese [Ehss-koh-SEHSS] The ancient Romans used to call the ancient Scots, Scotti. Like most places in the world, informations on the earliest inhabitants of the islands of Great Britain and Ireland are limited and shrouded in darkness. Some sources suggests the occupation of the isles by a non- Indo-European group of people called Iberians, which was followed by the arrival of the so-called Kelts an Indo-European people from the European mainland. Iberia is the older name for the Spanish peninsula. The Kelts were the first prehistoric people to rise from anonymity in

the European territories north of the Alps mountains. They dominated the western and central European scene right upto the advent and the rise of the Roman civilisation. Greeks used to call them Keltoi and the Romans called them Gauls. They had settled a great part of Europe extending from Ireland and Britain up to the region of Galatia in modern day Turkey. There is a possibility of further eastwards presence in Asia, along the northern slopes of Himalayas upto the Kam province of Tibet, Upper Burma and thence southwards into Assam and northwards towards Japan. Kelts held considerable political and military significance. But 15 they never presented a united front or ethnic group or a great empire, they were divided into many tribes with different dialects. They are an important factor in the development of a specifically European civilisation. As a people Kelts loved war and adventure, pleasure and feasts. The various people recorded and mentioned by the ancient Romans and others as Bretons, Scots, Gauls etc. were all Kelts!. In Spain, Kelts mixed with native Iberians to form the community of Keltiberians. One of the oldest recorded inhabitants of Scotland and possibly of Britain as a whole are the people known as Picts. The term comes from Latin picti meaning painted people as the Picts used to paint their bodies. Picts probably called themselves Cruithne. Information on the Picts are scanty and very few Pictish words have survived. The

Picts followed a matrillineal system of inheritence, a king's nephew rather than his son retains the throne. The exact affiliation of the Picts is not known but many authorities include them within the broader classification of the Keltic family of people. The Picts later on merged with the Scots to give an unified entity to the Scottish nationhood. The Scotland therefore was once known as the kingdom of the Scots and Picts. The Scots were settlers in Ireland, originally coming from the European mainland, who later on migrated in groups into the area of Scotland. There were other addition also to the diverse origin of the Scottish people from the coming of the Norsemen and Germanic tribes like the Angles. Bretons, another Keltic people, were also part of the ancient population of Scotland Keltic. tradition survives strongly in Ireland, Scottish Highlands, Wales, Isle of Man and the Brittany province of France. A Keltic substratum is however present throughout Europe from Iceland to Spain and from France to Germany and beyond. 'The comic book characters Asterix, Obelix and others created by Goscinny and Underzo is based on Keltic life-story. 16 17 The whole of British Isles, Ireland and the Britanny of France is full of megalithic and monolithic stones and stone structures, menhirs, cromlechs, dolmens etc. The Stonehenge of Salisbury plains is quite famous amongst them. The presence and the

association of the Kelts with such mouments is significant, which could represent a passover of tradition from some other older inhabitants yet undiscovered. The megalitic monuments of these islands and Brittany has definite similarities with those found in the Khasi hills. There is mention in the Roman records of the presence of a Cassi tribe of Bretons. At the time of the Roman invasion of Britain by Julius Caesar, this Cassi tribe led by their chief named Caswallon gave heroic resistance to the more well organised invaders. Like the Scots, the Cassi were also migrants to the island from the European mainland. Tuareg Across the Mediterrannean sea, opposite the European land mass, in the arid regions of north Africa dwell a people known as Tuareg. Tuaregs are a fair skinned nomadic warrior tribe, mostly of Caucasoid strain. Nowadays many of them have taken to settled life. The Tuareg male wears a veil leaving out only the eyes, the female however goes unveiled. The famous veil which they call /itham is wrapped round the head excluding the eyes A man begins wearing it from the age of puberty. They inhabit a wide area of Sahara and Sahel regions of northwestern Africa straddling four countries, sourthern Algeria, southwestern Libya, much of western Niger and northeastern Mali. Tuaregs are divided into seven major Kels or groups or septs, Kel Ahhagar, Kel Ajjer, Kel Adrar, Kel Air, Kel Geres,

Aullemeden Kel Dennek and Aullemeden Kel Ataram. Kel in their language denotes a group or community. Tuareg is a term derived from Arabic "Terek" meaning "those abandoned by 18 God". They call themselves Kel Tagelmoust meaning "the people of the veil". Tuaregs are muslim by religion but not Arab. The women of their community are free, with little restrictions, maintaining a good position in the society. The society itself is matrilineal, the inheritence following the female lines. Alongside them live a people of Negro origin who started as slaves of the Tuareg, known as Harratin. The Harratin also adopted the system of matriliny and practice it. They also wear the veil or litham. Tuaregs have their own system of writing, the script of which is known as Tifinagh or Tifinar. Many opine that it might have relation with the ancient Libyan or Egyptian form of writing. The way the word Kell is being used by these people, could give a clue as to the meaning of the word Kelt. Linguists have detected several similarities between Egyptian and Keltic languages. The Tuaregs may lie midway on that connecting line. Ravaged by the rigours of time and environment, they could represent a group identifiable as Keltic or proto-Keltic remnant. Historical records indicates the presence of Hindustani* mercenaries in the service of the Jaintia Kings, during the pre- British era, in small numbers. Epilogue Does the Khasis have some connection with the megalithic cultured people of Europe? The ancient stone monuments and structures which may be in the form of monoliths or other megaliths preserved to this day in Great Britain, Ireland and the Brittany province of France exhibits great similarity with structures and monuments seen in the Khasi hills. There are few other monolithic cultural spots around the world and not all of them have the Keltic stamp on them. So the speculated connection between the Khasi hills and the European megalithic cultural areas can be a mere co-incidence or it may not be so. The 50 congruences of language and the following of matrilineage by both the Khasis and the Picts also make some grounds of commonality. There also the point can be raised that this practice is found in several communities around the globe like the Pueblo Amerindians of North America, The Nair caste of Kerala state of India and the Menangkabu tribe of Indonesia. The French, Italian and the Spanish languages are Romance or Latinic languages ie. derived from Latin. Prior to this Latinisation, particularly in France and Spain a Keltic sub- stratum was present. A large number of Keltic originated words still persists in usage in French and also to some extent in Spanish. The French and Spanish word for Scotland and scotch may well be the ancient Keltic terms for them. Thus French

"Ecosse" pronounced ay-KUHSS meaning Scotland and "ecossais" pronounced ay-KUH-SEH meaning scotch, sounds very close to the words Khasi, Khas, Khas, Khastiu, Kasshu or Cossaei. Satyakam Phukan Guwahati, Assam January, 2006 PROLOGUE The hill tract lying between Bangladesh plains to the south and the Assam plains to the north forms the so called Garo, Khasi and the Jaintia hills, going fom west to east. This range of mountain becomes continous in the east with the Karbi Anglong and North Cachar hills of Assam which itself is connected to the Naga hills in the east. The Garo, Khasi and the Jaintia hills comprises the Indian state having a

Sanskritised name of Meghalaya meaning the abode of the clouds, much alike the Himalayas the home of ice or snow. The Khasi people ie. the Khasi proper and Jaintia and others inhabit the Khasi and Jaintia hills. There are few scattered communities of Khasis in the Karbi Anglong and North Cachar hills districts, Cachar district of Assam and also in Bangladesh. The Khasi country has three parts, the northern Bhoi region with extensive flat lands and valleys, having a gradual sloping towards the north. The central region is called the Ri-Lum. It has a higher elevation and is in the shape of an irregular plateau. The Shillong peak (6449 feet) is the highest point here. It also includes the central plateau of the Jaintia hills with small ranges of hills with wide and beautiful valleys within them. The southern War region is somewhat irregularly composed, having steep slopes, deep gorges, with a sudden descent down to the southern plains. The upper segment of the land presents a temperate climate but the border areas to the north and south have a warmer climate, corresponding to that of the adjacent plainsland. Cherrapunji or Sohra in the Khasi tongue is a rainy spot competitively exchanging place with a neighbouring village of Mawsynram for the title of the 'wettest place on earth’. Khasi is a general term for the various tribes and subtribes of the 1

ekejeqsdeayy jo deur qoyaHS © ae ete Wess ie Asad yTONVd Khasi and Jaintia hills. The Khynriams or Nonglums are the Khasi proper. They inhabit the middle range of hills and are composed of the Khynriam proper and their allied subtribes in the central plateau. The Pnar or Jaintia or Synteng occupy the central plateau of the Jaintia hills. The War sub-tribe live on the south. They include the Shella people and other allied groups, the Amwi people with their allied War-Synteng of the Southern Jaintia hills. The Bhois, both Khasi and Pnar dwell on the northern part of the Khasi and Jaintia hills. Lyngngams comprises a Garo admixed Khasi group dwelling on the westernmost and northwest edge of the Khasi hills. Several minor non-Khasi groups of people are interspersed in between. Majority of the Khasi people are fair and medium complexioned with an Austro-Mongoloid physiognomy and with very common sprinklings of Negroid and Caucasoid features. Khasi proper of the uplands are mostly brown or fair complexion, the Pnars and Bhois are however a bit darker and the Lyngngams a bit more. The overall appearence bear similarities with the Burmese (Myanmarese), Cambodian (Kampuchean), Malay and Palaung-Wa group of people of south-east Asia. However slanting eyes with prominent epicanthic folds and high check bones are less common and less pronounced in the Khasi's physical features, unlike the Mongoloids.

The Khasis practice a system of matriliny. The inheritance of the clanshood coming down the mother's side. This is a peculiarity which is not common with others. Most tribes and communities in the India's north-east are patrilineal. Those few among others to follow the system of matrilineage probably did so after coming in contact with the Khasis like the Hill Lalung or Hill Tiwa tribe of Assam and Meghalaya and the Garos of Meghalaya. The Khasis were in the habit of raising monoliths as commemorative or religious structures. These can be seen strewn all over the Khasi country in the form of menhirs, dolmens and other megaliths. The Konyak Naga tribe also used to indulge in 3 similar activities of erecting monoliths. A linguistic connection was noted by some scholars between the Khasi and Konyak languages and also with the Wanchoo (Vanchoo) tribe of Arunachal Pradesh state of India. The Khasi language alongwith it's various local variations is classed as an Austric language of the Mon-Khmer/Mon-Annam group. The Mon or Tailang are one of the earliest inhabitants of Burma (Myanmar) and represent an Austro-Asiatic segment of people admixed with early Telegu or Telinga immigrants from India. Khmer is another name for the Cambodians or Kampucheans. Annamese are the Vietnamese proper. They also show similarities with the Malay language and a similarity is highly probable with the Malagasy people of the Madagascar island, off the coast of Africa in the Indian occean.

Several linguistic and nomeclatural similarities have been noted between many Mon-Khmer speaking tribes of south-east Asia and the Khasis. Tribe names like Stieng and Bahner are congnate with the names Synteng and Pnar. Name of the tribe Wa is similar to the name War. The Wa tribe represents a comparatively primitive people inhabiting a widely scattered area in upper Burma (Myanmar), the Yunnan province of China and Thailand. They are divided into Lawa or "tame Wa", who are mostly Buddhist, adopting Shan (Tai) or Chinese customs and Kawa or the "Wild Wa" who are animist and were politically autonomous until quite recently. A vivid account of the "Wild Wa" of the recent times can be obtained from the book "The Land of Jade" by a Swedish writer Mr. Bertil Lintner. The book was written on a journey through Assam, Nagaland and across the border through Burma (Myanmar) into Thailand. The linguistic similarities are extensive, a few samples are given herewith. The Khasi language also have words dissimilar with the Austric languages and with striking similarity with languages placed far away in Asia, Europe and Africa, which seems more than mere co- incidence. The origin of the word "Khasi" as applicable to the Khasis is also something of a mystery. graush CHANNEL Sketch map of British Isles Scott, Scotland, Kelts David Scott was perhaps one of the first European to have visited the interiors of the Khasi hills. It was he who first initiated negotiations with a powerful Khasi chieftain, the Syiem of Nongkhlaw U Tirot Singh. The purpose was the construction of a north-south spanning road through the Khasi hills. The Assam plains and the eastern Bengal were by this time already within the confines of the British Raj. He travelled up the numerous footpaths known to Khasis as lynti-khasi to attend a conclave of Khasi chiefs. at Nongkhlaw. Employing porters to carry him, he spent three nights on the way to reach Nongkhlaw on the 3rd of November 1826, covering a distance of 60 miles. He was popular with the hillsfolk and has to his credit the introduction of potato, pears, cabbage and beet cultivation in the hills. Mother of U Tirot Singh Ka Ksan Syiem was particularly fond of this foreigner. She saved him during the sudden revolt of the Khasis, by warning him at the dead of a night. At the age of 45 years, Scott ended his life in his beloved Khasi hills at Cherrapunji in August 1831. His grave can be seen even today. Shillong in the central plateau land was made the military headquarters of the British in 1866 and in 1874 it was made the capital of the province of Assam. After the division of the Assam state and the creation of Meghalaya, Shillong has been the capital of

Meghalaya. Enthralled by its natural beauty, Khasi hills in general and Shillong in particular was called by the Britishers "The Scotland of the East". Scotland is the northernmost of the four countries (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) that comprise the United Kingdom. It is a hilly land with a cool climate and has several offshore islands within its boundaries. Divided into four regions Highlands, Lowlands, Southern Uplands and Islands, Scotland 14 makes up roughly one-third of the island of Great Britain. Scotland is the English name, the French, Italian and the Spanish have different terminology for the words Scotland and scotch : Scotland Scotch French Ecosse [ay-KUHSS] ecossais [ay-KUH-SEH] Italian Scozea [SKOH-ts_ yah] scozzese [Skoht-TSEH-seh] Spanish Escocia [ehss-KOH-S_ yah] escosese [Ehss-koh-SEHSS] The ancient Romans used to call the ancient Scots, Scotti. Like most places in the world, informations on the earliest inhabitants of the islands of Great Britain and Ireland are limited and shrouded in darkness. Some sources suggests the occupation of the isles by a non- Indo-European group of people called Iberians, which was followed by the arrival of the so-called Kelts an Indo-European people from the European mainland. Iberia is the older name for the Spanish peninsula. The Kelts were the first prehistoric people to rise from anonymity in

the European territories north of the Alps mountains. They dominated the western and central European scene right upto the advent and the rise of the Roman civilisation. Greeks used to call them Keltoi and the Romans called them Gauls. They had settled a great part of Europe extending from Ireland and Britain up to the region of Galatia in modern day Turkey. There is a possibility of further eastwards presence in Asia, along the northern slopes of Himalayas upto the Kam province of Tibet, Upper Burma and thence southwards into Assam and northwards towards Japan. Kelts held considerable political and military significance. But 15 they never presented a united front or ethnic group or a great empire, they were divided into many tribes with different dialects. They are an important factor in the development of a specifically European civilisation. As a people Kelts loved war and adventure, pleasure and feasts. The various people recorded and mentioned by the ancient Romans and others as Bretons, Scots, Gauls etc. were all Kelts!. In Spain, Kelts mixed with native Iberians to form the community of Keltiberians. One of the oldest recorded inhabitants of Scotland and possibly of Britain as a whole are the people known as Picts. The term comes from Latin picti meaning painted people as the Picts used to paint their bodies. Picts probably called themselves Cruithne. Information on the Picts are scanty and very few Pictish words have survived. The

Picts followed a matrillineal system of inheritence, a king's nephew rather than his son retains the throne. The exact affiliation of the Picts is not known but many authorities include them within the broader classification of the Keltic family of people. The Picts later on merged with the Scots to give an unified entity to the Scottish nationhood. The Scotland therefore was once known as the kingdom of the Scots and Picts. The Scots were settlers in Ireland, originally coming from the European mainland, who later on migrated in groups into the area of Scotland. There were other addition also to the diverse origin of the Scottish people from the coming of the Norsemen and Germanic tribes like the Angles. Bretons, another Keltic people, were also part of the ancient population of Scotland Keltic. tradition survives strongly in Ireland, Scottish Highlands, Wales, Isle of Man and the Brittany province of France. A Keltic substratum is however present throughout Europe from Iceland to Spain and from France to Germany and beyond. 'The comic book characters Asterix, Obelix and others created by Goscinny and Underzo is based on Keltic life-story. 16 17 The whole of British Isles, Ireland and the Britanny of France is full of megalithic and monolithic stones and stone structures, menhirs, cromlechs, dolmens etc. The Stonehenge of Salisbury plains is quite famous amongst them. The presence and the

association of the Kelts with such mouments is significant, which could represent a passover of tradition from some other older inhabitants yet undiscovered. The megalitic monuments of these islands and Brittany has definite similarities with those found in the Khasi hills. There is mention in the Roman records of the presence of a Cassi tribe of Bretons. At the time of the Roman invasion of Britain by Julius Caesar, this Cassi tribe led by their chief named Caswallon gave heroic resistance to the more well organised invaders. Like the Scots, the Cassi were also migrants to the island from the European mainland. Tuareg Across the Mediterrannean sea, opposite the European land mass, in the arid regions of north Africa dwell a people known as Tuareg. Tuaregs are a fair skinned nomadic warrior tribe, mostly of Caucasoid strain. Nowadays many of them have taken to settled life. The Tuareg male wears a veil leaving out only the eyes, the female however goes unveiled. The famous veil which they call /itham is wrapped round the head excluding the eyes A man begins wearing it from the age of puberty. They inhabit a wide area of Sahara and Sahel regions of northwestern Africa straddling four countries, sourthern Algeria, southwestern Libya, much of western Niger and northeastern Mali. Tuaregs are divided into seven major Kels or groups or septs, Kel Ahhagar, Kel Ajjer, Kel Adrar, Kel Air, Kel Geres,

Aullemeden Kel Dennek and Aullemeden Kel Ataram. Kel in their language denotes a group or community. Tuareg is a term derived from Arabic "Terek" meaning "those abandoned by 18 God". They call themselves Kel Tagelmoust meaning "the people of the veil". Tuaregs are muslim by religion but not Arab. The women of their community are free, with little restrictions, maintaining a good position in the society. The society itself is matrilineal, the inheritence following the female lines. Alongside them live a people of Negro origin who started as slaves of the Tuareg, known as Harratin. The Harratin also adopted the system of matriliny and practice it. They also wear the veil or litham. Tuaregs have their own system of writing, the script of which is known as Tifinagh or Tifinar. Many opine that it might have relation with the ancient Libyan or Egyptian form of writing. The way the word Kell is being used by these people, could give a clue as to the meaning of the word Kelt. Linguists have detected several similarities between Egyptian and Keltic languages. The Tuaregs may lie midway on that connecting line. Ravaged by the rigours of time and environment, they could represent a group identifiable as Keltic or proto-Keltic remnant. The remnants of the older settlers are represented by people known 60 as Dards, who form a significant minority in Ladakh. These facts and the similarities could mean that the commonality of dresses and words are leftovers of the influence of one group of people who also contributed in the formation of the Khasi people or they may be acquisitions by these same people on their way eastwards. Streams converge from varying sources and directions to fuse and form a river. Likewise people from different origins, coming from different directions unite to form various nationalities. They mix, fuse and conglomerate into entire new sets of people. Migrations in the ancient times were a time consuming affair often dictated by compulsions of a prevailing circumstance. Hostilities and enslavements were also common. The migrants often had to confront the nature in its mild or extreme forms. They also had to encounter different types of people, both akin and alien, on the way. There may be stopovers enroute at some places, temporarily residing alongside alien people. They may halt in some places for years together, before resuming their onwards march towards the final settling place. Again a section of them may choose to settle down at such temporary stoppages.

Considerable social, cultural and linguistic exchanges took place from the intermingling of different groups of people. It would not be in the wrong, if it is said that the ancient peoples mixed up like anything leaving only a few isolated communities in an unmixed state.
